First Wings

Dawn spilled gold across the mountain peaks as the little dragon stepped to the edge of the world.

His nest—woven from pine boughs, soft moss, and his mother's shed scales that shimmered like old coins—sat high on a cliff where his kind had awakened for a thousand years. Below, the valley slept beneath a quilt of mist. Above, the sky waited: vast, blue, and terribly empty.

"Must I?" he whispered. No one answered, but his mother watched from a nearby ledge, her ancient eyes holding a patience older than stone. She knew, as all mothers know, that some journeys cannot be taken together.

The little dragon unfolded his wings. They trembled like autumn leaves, their thin membranes catching the morning light and glowing amber and rose. All his short life, those wings had been mere ornaments—beautiful, useless things folded against his back like closed fans. Now they were supposed to carry him. Now they were supposed to know the way.

He remembered the old stories: dragons who danced with storms, who stitched clouds together in their passing, who drank straight from the cup of the sky. Then he looked down at the ground, so far below, waiting with its hard and honest stones.

The wind rose then, as though it had been listening. It pressed cool, curious fingers against his face, and something stirred deep in his chest—an old music, a memory he had never lived. His heart quickened. His claws loosened on the rock.

He jumped.

For one endless moment, he fell. The world blurred; terror sang in his ears; the valley rushed up to claim him. But then instinct—ancient as fire—woke in his wings. They opened. They caught the wind the way a sail catches the sea, and falling became floating, and floating became flight.

Oh, the wonder of it!

The wind combed his scales with careful fingers. The mist parted before him in silken ribbons. Below, the world he had feared unfolded like a map of miracles: rivers of silver, forests of green velvet, fields embroidered with wildflowers. He was not falling out of the sky; he was belonging to it.

He laughed, and out came a small puff of smoke—his very first. He climbed higher, drunk on altitude, while the rising sun set his wings ablaze with ruby, topaz, and flame. For the first time, he understood what the elder dragons meant when they spoke his name: *one who carries the morning*.

Far behind, his mother lifted silently into the air to follow, her great wings steady, her heart full.

And the little dragon flew—clumsy, radiant, and free—into the vast blue pages of his own beginning.

title: 健康饮食
text:
Here is a practical, step-by-step healthy eating guide in English.

---

 A Practical Guide to Healthy Eating

 Step 1: Know Your Personal Needs
- Consider your age, gender, activity level, and health goals (e.g., weight loss, muscle gain, maintenance).
- Consult a doctor or dietitian if you have special conditions like diabetes, allergies, or digestive issues.

 Step 2: Plan Your Meals Ahead
- Plan meals and snacks for the week.
- Make a grocery list before shopping to avoid impulse buying.
- Prepare ingredients in advance, such as washing vegetables or cooking grains.

 Step 3: Build a Balanced Plate
At each main meal, aim for:
- ½ plate vegetables and fruits — different colors for different nutrients.
- ¼ plate whole grains or starchy carbs — brown rice, oats, quinoa, whole-wheat bread, sweet potatoes.
- ¼ plate protein — fish, chicken, eggs, beans, tofu, or lean meat.

 Step 4: Choose Whole Foods Over Processed Foods
- Eat foods closest to their natural form.
- Limit packaged snacks, fast food, sugary cereals, and instant noodles.
- Read food labels and avoid products with long ingredient lists.

 Step 5: Eat Enough Protein
- Include protein at every meal to support muscles and keep you full.
- Good options: eggs, Greek yogurt, lentils, fish, chicken, tofu, nuts.

 Step 6: Don’t Fear Healthy Fats
- Choose unsaturated fats: olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish.
- Limit trans fats and reduce saturated fats from fried foods and fatty meats.

 Step 7: Focus on Fiber
- Eat whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and fruits daily.
- Fiber helps digestion, controls blood sugar, and keeps you satisfied.

 Step 8: Stay Hydrated
- Drink water throughout the day, about 6–8 glasses or more if active.
- Limit sugary drinks, energy drinks, and excessive alcohol.
- Herbal teas and infused water are good alternatives.

 Step 9: Watch Portion Sizes
- Use smaller plates and bowls.
- Listen to your body and stop eating when you are about 80% full.
- Avoid eating straight from large packages.

 Step 10: Reduce Added Sugar and Salt
- Limit sweets, sugary drinks, and desserts.
- Flavor food with herbs, spices, lemon, and garlic instead of too much salt.
- Check labels for hidden sugars and sodium.

 Step 11: Practice Mindful Eating
- Eat slowly and chew thoroughly.
- Avoid screens during meals.
- Pay attention to hunger and fullness cues.

 Step 12: Cook More at Home
- Home-cooked meals usually have less salt, sugar, and unhealthy fat.
- Try simple cooking methods: steaming, grilling, baking, stir-frying with little oil.

 Step 13: Allow Flexibility
- Healthy eating is not about perfection.
- It is okay to enjoy treats occasionally — aim for balance, not restriction.

 Step 14: Be Consistent
- Small, daily habits matter more than extreme diets.
- Progress takes time, so stay patient and keep going.

---

 Quick Example of a Healthy Day

- Breakfast: Oatmeal with berries, nuts, and a boiled egg  
- Lunch: Grilled chicken, quinoa, and mixed vegetable salad  
- Snack: Greek yogurt or an apple with peanut butter  
- Dinner: Baked salmon, brown rice, and steamed broccoli  
- Drinks: Water, green tea

---

Remember: The best diet is the one you can follow long-term while feeling good, energetic, and satisfied.

title: 坚持的意义
text:
The Meaning of Persistence

Persistence is commonly defined as the ability to continue firmly in a course of action despite difficulty or delay. Yet its true significance runs far deeper than mere stubbornness; it is the quiet, invisible bridge that connects intention to achievement.

History repeatedly teaches us that greatness is rarely the product of raw talent alone. Thomas Edison endured thousands of unsuccessful attempts before the lightbulb finally glowed. J.K. Rowling received numerous rejections before the wizarding world captivated millions. These stories remind us that persistence is not the absence of failure, but the refusal to let failure write the final chapter. Each setback becomes a lesson, and every obstacle, when met with determination, transforms into a stepping stone.

On a more personal level, persistence is the sculptor of character. When we commit to showing up every day—whether learning a language, mastering an instrument, or pursuing a distant career goal—we enter into a meaningful dialogue with our better selves. Progress is seldom dramatic; rather, it is the compound interest of small, consistent efforts. Just as a river carves a canyon not through force, but through unyielding patience, our daily dedication slowly shapes the life we aspire to live.

In an age obsessed with speed and instant gratification, persistence offers a different wisdom: that everything truly worthwhile requires time. It teaches resilience, deepens our sense of purpose, and reveals that the journey itself is as valuable as the destination. To persist is, ultimately, to maintain faith—not only in the goal ahead, but in our own capacity to reach it.

title: 中学生时间管理
text:

---

 Milo and the Land of Later

Once upon a time, in a little town where the rooftops touched the evening mist, there lived a twelve-year-old boy named Milo. Milo was bright, curious, and kind — but he had a favorite word, and that word was "later."

"I'll finish my homework *later*," he'd say, dropping his schoolbag by the door.
"I'll tidy my room *later*," he'd mumble, stepping over a mountain of socks.
"I'll read that book *later*," he'd yawn, reaching for his video games instead.

And so, every night, Milo went to bed with his tasks undone, and every morning he woke up feeling like he was already behind.

One quiet evening, as the moon climbed over the hills, Milo heard a tiny sound coming from his desk.

*Tick... tick... squeak!*

He leaned closer to his old alarm clock, and to his amazement, a tiny door swung open in its side. Out stepped a mouse no bigger than a thimble, wearing a silver waistcoat and carrying a lantern that glowed like a firefly.

"Good evening," said the mouse, bowing politely. "I'm Minnie the Minute Mouse, and I've come to collect you."

"Collect me?" Milo blinked. "For what?"

"Why, for all your 'laters,' of course!" squeaked Minnie. "They've been piling up for years. Someone must take care of them — and tonight, that someone is you."

Before Milo could say "later" again, the clock's hands began to spin, the room swirled like water going down a drain, and — *whoosh!* — Milo found himself standing in a strange grey land.

As far as he could see, there were mountains. Mountains of unopened books. Towers of unfinished homework. A river of melting ice cream that no one had eaten in time. And everywhere, drifting like lost balloons, were shimmering bubbles, each whispering in Milo's own voice: *"Later... later... later..."*

"What is this place?" Milo whispered.

"This," said a slow, deep voice, "is the Land of Later."

Milo turned around. Sitting on a throne made of old calendars was a great grey owl, with spectacles perched on her beak and a cloak sewn from bits of midnight sky.

"I am Olivia, the Keeper of Hours," said the owl. "Every minute you set aside for 'later' floats here. Some children lose only a few. But you, Milo..." She sighed a feathery sigh. "Yours have built mountains."

Milo felt very small. "I didn't know they were... real."

"Oh, they're real," said Olivia gently. "But don't despair. Would you like to know a secret? Every mountain here can be moved — one pebble at a time."

"One pebble?"

Olivia spread her great wings. "Watch."

She picked up the tiniest pebble from the homework mountain — a single math problem — and placed it in Milo's hand. The moment he solved it, the pebble turned into a golden star and flew up into the sky, where it twinkled brightly.

"You see," said the owl, "time well spent becomes starlight. It never truly leaves you. But time pushed aside becomes grey fog — and fog helps no one."

Then Olivia taught Milo the Three Secrets of the Hours.

"First, eat your frog first." Milo giggled, but the owl nodded seriously. "Do the hardest, most important task while your mind is fresh. The rest of the day will taste sweeter."

"Second, break big mountains into small pebbles. A whole book is heavy, but one chapter is light. A whole room is messy, but one corner is easy."

"Third — and listen carefully, for children always forget this one — rest is not wasted time. Sleep, play, and daydreaming are the soil where tomorrow's energy grows. A wise keeper of hours plans for rest, too."

Milo nodded slowly. Somewhere deep inside, he had always known these things. But now they glowed in his mind like the golden stars above.

"Now," said Olivia, "it's time to go home. Your bed is waiting — and a good night's sleep is the very first task of every wise day."

Minnie waved her lantern, the clock hands spun backwards, and — *whoosh!* — Milo was back in his room. Moonlight lay soft and silver on his desk.

The next morning, Milo did something new. He ate his frog first: homework, finished before dinner. He broke mountains into pebbles: one corner of his room, tidied in ten minutes. And when the stars came out, he climbed into bed without a single "later" left hanging over his head.

From the little door in his clock came a tiny, satisfied *squeak*.

And if you listen very carefully on quiet nights, you might hear it too — the sound of a minute well spent, turning into starlight.

The End. 🌙

---

1. 先做最难、最重要的事（"吃青蛙"法则）
2. 把大任务拆成小步骤
3. 休息也是时间管理的一部分——这一点特意呼应睡前场景，让孩子安心入睡

title: 科技改变生活
text:
The Garden in Blue

Lina hadn’t seen the color blue in three years. Macular degeneration had stolen the edges from her world first, then the center, until her garden became a blur of green ghosts. She still watered it by memory, fingers finding stems she could no longer distinguish.

Then came ARIA.

It arrived in a plain white box from the hospital: a pair of lightweight glasses, two temples that hummed when she put them on. “Augmented Reality for Impaired Anatomy,” the technician said, adjusting the bridge. “It won’t cure your eyes, but it will redraw what they miss.”

She doubted it. For weeks the device sat on the kitchen counter like an unanswered question.

The morning she finally wore it, the world rebuilt itself.

At first it was only contrast: dark soil against pale paving stones, the sharp line of the fence. Then color bled back in. The hydrangeas were not merely pale shapes; they were violet, indigo, a blue so deep it felt like falling into water. Lina stood still, tears warm on her cheeks, afraid that moving would break the spell.

But ARIA did not break. It labeled, it clarified, it stabilized. When her hand reached for a trowel, the tool glowed softly at the edges. When she walked toward the steps, a faint amber path appeared, warning of the drop. The machine did not replace her vision; it negotiated with her blindness, sentence by sentence.

Her granddaughter, Mei, video-called that evening. For the first time in years, Lina could see the freckles across the girl’s nose, the new silver ring in her ear. “Grandma, you’re looking right at me,” Mei said, voice cracking.

“It’s the glasses,” Lina whispered.

“It’s not the glasses,” Mei said.

Her neighbor paused at the fence the next morning; for the first time in months, Lina recognized the worry lines beside his eyes before he spoke.

Lina began to paint again. The old easel came down from the attic, crusted with ochre and umber. With ARIA’s guidance she mixed blues she could not perceive unaided, trusting the numbers that floated beside her palette: cobalt 72%, titanium white 18%. Each stroke was a collaboration between memory and algorithm. The result was awkward in places, luminous in others. She hung the first canvas—a vase of hydrangeas—where the morning light would catch it. She started a small online gallery. Strangers bought her work, unaware of the quiet partnership behind each canvas.

Not everything was restored. Night remained difficult; crowds still unnerved her; the device needed charging, updating, occasional rebooting. And there were days she removed the glasses on purpose, letting the blur return so she could remember what she had lost and what she had gained.

On the afternoon of her seventy-fifth birthday, Lina sat in her garden without the device. The world was soft, watercolor, unfinished. But she knew the hydrangeas were blue. She did not need to see them to believe it.

Technology had not given her back her eyes. It had given her back her certainty—that color existed, that faces held detail, that she could still create something true. The garden remained imperfect, fragile, hers.

And that, she decided, was enough.

title: 感恩父母
text:
The Eternal Debt: Why Gratitude to Parents Is the Foundation of Our Humanity

From the moment we draw our first breath, there exists a love that asks for no contract, signs no terms, and yet pays every cost. It is the love of our parents—a love measured not in grand gestures, but in a thousand invisible sacrifices: lullabies hummed through fevers, career dreams quietly shelved, and palms held steady until our own feet found the ground. In an age that celebrates individual achievement and self-reliance, we often forget that our very capacity to stand was built upon the backs of those who chose to kneel beside us. Gratitude to parents is not merely a cultural courtesy; it is the cornerstone of moral maturity and the first true lesson in learning how to love unconditionally.

To understand why this gratitude is essential, one must first recognize the asymmetrical nature of parental devotion. Unlike most relationships in life, which operate on a principle of reciprocity, the bond between parent and child begins as profoundly one-sided. Parents pour into us their time, their resources, and their emotional energy during the very years when we are least capable of appreciation. They absorb our adolescent rebellion, our thoughtless words, and our relentless pursuit of independence without withdrawing their support. This is not to suggest that parenthood is a transaction demanding repayment; rather, it is to acknowledge that such unearned generosity creates a debt of the heart—a debt that cannot be settled, only honored. Recognizing this imbalance cultivates humility, the virtue that checks our ego and reminds us that we did not arrive at adulthood solely by our own merit.

Furthermore, gratitude toward parents serves as the seedbed for all other virtues. Cicero once wrote that gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others. When we learn to appreciate the sacrifices made by our parents, we develop the emotional vocabulary to recognize sacrifice in others: the teacher who stays after class, the friend who listens at midnight, the stranger who holds a door. Conversely, a life that fails to honor its origins often drifts toward narcissism, viewing the world as a marketplace of entitlement rather than a web of interdependence. In this sense, thanking our parents is not an act of looking backward; it is the necessary posture for moving forward into society as compassionate, grounded individuals.

Yet, in the modern narrative, gratitude is too often confused with material repayment. We send money, pay for vacations, or purchase the latest gadgets, mistaking these transactions for connection. True gratitude, however, is an active practice of understanding. It means seeing our parents not as immutable figures from childhood, but as flawed, aging individuals who carried their own unspoken fears and broken dreams. It means forgiving the mistakes they made while raising us, knowing they navigated uncharted waters without a manual. Most importantly, it manifests in presence—the patience to teach them technology they do not grasp, the willingness to listen to stories we have heard a hundred times, and the courage to hold their hands as they once held ours.

In conclusion, the gratitude we owe our parents is the eternal debt that enriches the borrower. It does not impoverish us to acknowledge how deeply we have been given; rather, it completes us. As our parents once slowed their pace to match our stumbling steps, we must now adjust our stride to theirs. To honor them is not to engage in a duty bound by obligation, but to participate in the timeless cycle of love—one that began with them, but only reaches its full meaning when we, in turn, learn to give without keeping score.

title: 夏洛的网
text:
The Web That Teaches Us About Friendship
 A Speech on *Charlotte's Web*

Good morning, everyone.

Today, I want to talk about a spider. Not a scary spider, but one of the greatest friends in all of literature. Her name is Charlotte, and she lives in the pages of E.B. White's timeless classic, *Charlotte's Web*.

The Story

For those who may not remember, the story begins on a farm, where a little girl named Fern saves a runt piglet from being killed. She names him Wilbur and raises him with love. But when Wilbur grows too big, he is sold to her uncle's farm, where he learns a terrible truth: pigs like him are destined to become bacon and ham.

Wilbur is terrified. He cries out that he doesn't want to die. And then, from the darkness of the barn, comes a small, calm voice: "I will save you."

That voice belongs to Charlotte, a grey spider. Through her cleverness and devotion, she weaves words into her web — "Some Pig," "Terrific," "Radiant," "Humble" — convincing the humans that Wilbur is extraordinary. Wilbur's life is spared, but Charlotte, having given everything she had, quietly passes away, leaving behind only her egg sac and the memory of her love.

Lesson One: True Friendship Asks for Nothing in Return

The heart of this story is a friendship that expects no reward. Near the end, Wilbur asks Charlotte why she did so much for him, saying, "I don't deserve it. I've never done anything for you." Charlotte answers with one of the most beautiful lines ever written: *"You have been my friend. That in itself is a tremendous thing."*

Think about that. Charlotte didn't save Wilbur because he was useful, or popular, or could pay her back. She saved him simply because he was her friend. In a world where relationships are often measured by what we can gain, Charlotte reminds us that the purest friendship is given freely — and that being someone's friend is, in itself, a reason to act with love.

Lesson Two: Words Have Power

Charlotte's only weapon is her web — and her words. With just a few carefully chosen phrases, she changes how everyone sees Wilbur. He is no longer an ordinary pig headed for slaughter; he becomes "Some Pig," "Terrific," "Radiant."

This is a powerful lesson for all of us. Our words shape how others see themselves and how the world sees them. A kind word can lift someone up; a cruel one can tear them down. Charlotte used her words to save a life. Every day, we have the same choice — to use our words to build, to heal, and to encourage.

Lesson Three: Love Outlives Loss

Charlotte's death is heartbreaking, and E.B. White doesn't hide it from young readers. But the story doesn't end in despair. Charlotte's children hatch in the spring, and a few of them stay in the barn with Wilbur, continuing the circle of friendship.

This teaches us something profound about life and legacy: those we love may leave us, but the love itself remains. It lives on in memory, in the lives they touched, and in the new beginnings they made possible.

Conclusion

*Charlotte's Web* may look like a simple children's book about a pig and a spider, but it carries lessons that last a lifetime: cherish your friends, choose your words wisely, and trust that love endures beyond loss.

So let me leave you with this question: Who is your Charlotte — the friend who has stood by you without asking anything in return? And perhaps more importantly — whose Charlotte will you be?

May we all learn to weave webs of kindness, one word, one act of friendship at a time.

Thank you.

title: 小王子
text:
A Practical Guide to *The Little Prince*

Follow these steps to read, understand, and apply the lessons of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's *The Little Prince* to your daily life.

---

 Step 1: Read the Book with the Right Mindset
- Approach it as both a children's story and a philosophical book for adults.
- Read slowly. The story is short, but every chapter contains a hidden lesson.
- Keep a notebook nearby to write down quotes or moments that make you think.

---

 Step 2: Understand the Main Characters
| Character | What They Represent | Lesson |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| The Little Prince | Innocence, curiosity, pure love | Don't lose your inner child. |
| The Rose | Love, pride, vulnerability | Love requires patience and responsibility. |
| The Fox | Friendship, attachment, wisdom | True bonds take time to build. |
| The Aviator | Adult imagination, loneliness | Never fully abandon your creativity. |
| The Businessman, King, Drunkard, etc. | Flaws of grown-ups | Don't become obsessed with power, numbers, or appearances. |

---

 Step 3: Learn the Key Lessons
1. "What is essential is invisible to the eye."
   - Value feelings, trust, and love more than physical appearance or wealth.
2. "You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed."
   - Commitment matters in relationships, friendships, and care for others.
3. Beware of "serious matters."
   - Adults often focus on numbers, status, and productivity. Don't let these replace joy and wonder.
4. Tame your relationships.
   - Invest time and attention to make people special to you.

---

 Step 4: Apply the Lessons to Real Life

 In Relationships
- Spend quality time with people instead of just giving gifts.
- Be patient with people you love, even when they are difficult (like the Rose).
- Tell the people who matter that they are important to you.

 At Work or School
- Don't measure everything by numbers, grades, or money.
- Ask yourself: *Does this task truly matter to me or others?*

 In Daily Life
- Look at ordinary things with curiosity, like a child would.
- Take time to watch a sunset, look at the stars, or care for a plant.
- Don't rush. The Little Prince traveled slowly and learned deeply.

---

 Step 5: Use the Book in Difficult Moments
- When you feel lonely: Remember the stars. Someone, somewhere, cares about you.
- When you miss someone: Look at what you shared, not just the loss.
- When life feels meaningless: Ask yourself what you have "tamed" and what you are responsible for.

---

 Step 6: Share It with Others
- Give the book as a gift to a friend, child, or loved one.
- Read it aloud with someone and discuss what each chapter means.
- Use quotes from the book in letters, cards, or speeches.

---

 Quick Checklist
- [ ] Read *The Little Prince* at least once.
- [ ] Identify one character that reminds you of yourself.
- [ ] Find one person you want to "tame" or deepen your bond with.
- [ ] Practice seeing the invisible: kindness, trust, love, and time.
- [ ] Re-read the book every few years; it will feel different as you grow older.

---

 Final Thought
*The Little Prince* is not just a story to finish. It is a reminder to stay kind, curious, and human in a busy world. Read it with your heart, not only your eyes.

title: 家乡的春节
text:
Spring Festival in My Hometown

Spring Festival, also known as Chinese New Year, is the most important and joyful festival in my hometown. It usually falls in January or February, and the whole town comes alive with color, laughter, and the smell of delicious food.

A few days before the festival, every family starts to get ready. We clean our houses thoroughly to sweep away bad luck, and put up red couplets on the doors and paper cuttings on the windows. Red lanterns hang along the streets, making the town look warm and festive.

On New Year's Eve, the whole family gathers together for a big reunion dinner. In my hometown, dumplings are a must-have dish, because they symbolize wealth and good fortune. After dinner, we watch the Spring Festival Gala on TV, and at midnight, fireworks light up the sky. Children are especially happy because they receive red envelopes filled with lucky money from their elders.

During the following days, we visit relatives and friends, exchanging greetings like "Happy New Year" and "Good luck." Temple fairs and dragon dances add even more excitement to the holiday.

For me, Spring Festival is more than just a holiday. It is a time for family, love, and hope. No matter where I go in the future, the Spring Festival in my hometown will always hold a special place in my heart.

title: 傲慢与偏见
text:
The Proud Prince and the Clever Girl  
*A gentle fairy tale inspired by Pride and Prejudice*

Once upon a time, in a little village painted with green hills and golden buttercups, there lived a bright and kind girl named Lizzy. She loved to laugh, loved to read stories under old oak trees, and loved her family more than anything in the world.

One sunny morning, a grand carriage rolled into the village. Out stepped Prince Darcy. He wore a velvet coat, shiny boots, and a very serious face.

The villagers whispered, “He must be important!”

At the village fair, Lizzy saw the Prince. She smiled and said, “Good morning! Would you like to try some apple cider?”

Prince Darcy looked at her simple dress, then at her muddy boots, and frowned. “I do not talk to just anyone,” he said, and turned away.

Lizzy’s cheeks turned pink. “Well!” she said to her sister. “That prince is very proud. He thinks he is better than everyone.”

From that day on, Lizzy decided she did not like Prince Darcy. And Prince Darcy decided that Lizzy was too cheerful, too loud, and much too plain for a prince.

But the village was small, and the two kept meeting.

At the flower festival, Lizzy danced with a handsome soldier named Mr. Wickham. He smiled sweetly and told her, “Prince Darcy was very mean to me long ago.”

Lizzy believed him at once. “See?” she told her friends. “The Prince is not only proud—he is unkind!”

But Lizzy did not know the whole story.

One rainy afternoon, Lizzy was walking through the woods when she heard a soft whinny. Prince Darcy’s horse had slipped in the mud, and the Prince was trying to help it stand.

Lizzy ran over. “Hold his head gently,” she said. “I will lift his leg.”

Together, they helped the horse. The Prince’s fancy coat was covered in mud, but he did not complain. When they finished, he looked at Lizzy with surprised eyes.

“You are very brave,” he said quietly.

“And you are very muddy,” Lizzy giggled.

For the first time, Prince Darcy smiled. It was a small smile, but it was real.

Later, Lizzy learned something important. Mr. Wickham had not told the truth. He had caused trouble, and Prince Darcy had only tried to protect his family. Lizzy’s face grew hot. “I was wrong to judge him so quickly,” she said.

That night, there was a great ball at the palace. Lizzy wore a simple blue dress, but she shone like a star because she was kind and happy.

Prince Darcy walked across the room. He bowed low.

“Lizzy,” he said, “I have been proud. I looked at your dress and your cottage and thought I knew who you were. But I was wrong. You are clever and brave and good.”

Lizzy curtsied. “And I thought you were only proud and unkind,” she said. “But I did not look carefully enough. I am sorry, too.”

The Prince smiled. “May I have this dance?”

Lizzy took his hand. “Yes. But only if you promise to dance like a regular person, not like a stiff statue.”

Prince Darcy laughed—a big, happy laugh that made everyone turn and smile.

They danced under twinkling lanterns, and the whole village clapped. From that night on, Prince Darcy learned to be humble, and Lizzy learned to look deeper before judging others.

And so, the proud prince and the clever girl became the very best of friends. They planted gardens, helped the village, and read stories under the old oak tree together.

They lived happily ever after.

The End

*Sweet dreams, little one. Remember: never judge someone by the mud on their boots or the crown on their head. The kindest hearts are found when we look a little closer.*

title: 失败是成功之母
text:
下面是一个约500词的英文短篇故事：

The Glitch That Built the Champion

Maya’s hands shook as she set R-9 on the starting mat. Months of solder burns and sleepless nights had led to this moment—the National Robotics Qualifier. The whistle blew. R-9 lurched forward, sensors blinking, then spun in a wild circle and collided with the boundary wall. The crowd gasped. Maya rushed to the console, but lines of error code cascaded down the screen like digital rain. Round one: disqualified.

Back in her garage workshop, Maya stared at the scattered components. Failure clung to her like solder smoke. Her grandmother entered with tea. “A pot,” she said, “cracks before the kiln makes it strong.” Maya almost laughed; ceramic wisdom felt useless beside a smoking circuit board.

But the next morning she opened her notebook and wrote a single line: *Failure is data.* She rewatched the match video frame by frame. The crash wasn’t bad luck; it was a sensor calibration flaw compounded by untested code. She mapped every misstep: the wheel encoder miscounted, the ultrasonic sensor chattered near corners, and the autonomous loop panicked when obstacles appeared faster than predicted.

Instead of rebuilding the whole robot, Maya designed controlled failures. She built a miniature maze in the garage and let R-9 fail hundreds of times, logging each crash. She learned that failure wasn’t the opposite of success; it was the path to it. Every dent in the chassis taught her something no textbook could.

Her friends invited her to movies; she declined. Her younger brother teased that she was dating a robot. But slowly, R-9’s movements grew precise. It learned to pause, recalibrate, and choose alternate routes.

A year later, Maya stood again at the national finals. The arena was larger, the lights hotter. The task required the robot to navigate a maze, sort colored blocks, and rescue a dummy “survivor.” The whistle blew. R-9 glided forward, sensors steady. At one corner, an unexpected shadow confused the camera. For a heartbeat, Maya felt last year’s panic. But R-9 paused, rotated, and recalibrated—exactly as it had been taught by a hundred garage crashes.

It completed every stage with quiet efficiency. When the final score flashed—first place—the crowd erupted. Maya lifted the trophy, but her eyes drifted to the dented practice chassis sitting on the judges’ display table, the one she had insisted be shown.

“This trophy,” she said into the microphone, “belongs to every version that broke. They didn’t fail. They taught.”

In the garage that night, she opened her notebook to a fresh page and wrote: *Success is just failure that refused to quit.* Outside, the city lights hummed, and somewhere in the dark, the next prototype was already waiting to fall, rise, and learn.

---

title: 小狐狸与月亮
text:
A Timeless Tale of Wonder and Connection: Reflections on *The Little Fox and the Moon*

Reading *The Little Fox and the Moon* feels like wrapping oneself in a soft, moonlit blanket on a quiet autumn night. On the surface, it is a deceptively simple children's story about a young fox who gazes up at the night sky and discovers an unexpected friendship with the moon. Yet beneath its gentle prose and delicate illustrations lies a profound meditation on loneliness, longing, and the quiet beauty of connections that transcend distance.

What struck me most deeply was the story's tender exploration of solitude. The little fox, often wandering alone through the silver-dusted forest, initially looks to the moon out of curiosity. Gradually, this nightly ritual evolves into something resembling a conversation—one that requires no words, only presence. In an age of constant digital noise, the book reminds us that companionship does not always demand physical proximity or immediate reciprocity. Sometimes, the most comforting presence is simply the one that faithfully appears above the treetops, night after night, listening without interrupting.

The moon itself is a brilliant narrative choice. It is forever out of reach, yet perpetually radiant. Through the fox's innocent admiration, the story teaches a bittersweet but essential lesson about love and desire: not everything precious is meant to be possessed. The fox never tries to chase or capture the moon. Instead, he learns to appreciate its glow from afar, finding joy in the shared silence between earth and sky. This is a wisdom that resonates far beyond childhood—the understanding that some forms of beauty are made more sacred by their mystery and distance.

Ultimately, *The Little Fox and the Moon* is more than a bedtime story. It is an invitation to look up, to embrace wonder, and to recognize that even in our loneliest moments, we are seen. Whether you are five or fifty, this book leaves you with a quiet warmth in your chest and a sudden urge to step outside and say goodnight to the moon.

title: 中学生时间管理
text:
Title: Master Your Time, Master Your Life

Good morning, teachers and fellow students,

Today, I want to talk about something we all have in common: time. Every one of us gets exactly 24 hours a day—no more, no less. Yet some students seem to finish homework, enjoy hobbies, and still get enough sleep, while others always feel rushed and stressed. The difference is not talent; it is time management.

As middle school students, we are busier than ever. Classes, homework, exams, club activities, sports, family time, and friends all compete for our attention. Without a plan, it is easy to feel overwhelmed. But here is the good news: time management is a skill, and like any skill, it can be learned.

First, set clear goals. Ask yourself every day: “What is the most important thing I need to finish today?” When you have a clear target, you waste less time wondering what to do next.

Second, make a schedule. Use a planner, a calendar, or even a simple to-do list on your phone. Write down homework deadlines, test dates, and after-school activities. Planning helps you see the big picture and avoid last-minute panic.

Third, prioritize your tasks. Not everything is equally important. Do the hardest or most urgent task first when your energy is high. This is called “eating the frog.” Once you finish the difficult thing, the rest of your day will feel easier.

Fourth, break big tasks into small steps. A huge project can feel scary, but if you divide it into small parts and do a little each day, you will be amazed at how much you can achieve.

Fifth, avoid distractions. We all know how easy it is to pick up our phones and lose 30 minutes on social media. When you study, put your phone in another room or turn off notifications. Focus for 25 minutes, then take a 5-minute break. This method, called the Pomodoro Technique, really works.

Finally, remember to rest. Good time management is not about working every minute. Your brain needs sleep, exercise, and fun to stay healthy and productive. A balanced schedule actually helps you study better.

In conclusion, time is the one resource we can never get back. By setting goals, making plans, prioritizing tasks, avoiding distractions, and taking care of ourselves, we can use our time wisely. Let us stop saying “I don’t have time” and start saying “I will make time.”

Thank you.

title: 提高睡眠质量
text:
以下是一篇关于提高睡眠质量的英文散文，语言较为优美抒情：

---

 The Quiet Alchemy of Sleep

Sleep is not a small death, nor a passive folding of the day into darkness. It is, rather, a secret journey—a tender alchemy in which the body gathers its scattered threads and the mind rinses itself clean of noise. Yet in our age of glowing screens and restless ambition, sleep has become something we steal at the edges of midnight, a fugitive pleasure rather than a sacred rite. To sleep well is to remember that rest is not the opposite of labor, but its completion.

The first step toward better sleep is the simplest and the hardest: we must make peace with the setting sun. Our bodies are ancient instruments, tuned to the slow music of light and shadow. When evening arrives, let the lamps grow dim and amber; let the blue glare of phones retreat like a tide. Draw the curtains not as a barrier against the world, but as an invitation to the self. In that softened darkness, the brain begins to hum its lullaby, releasing the sweet chemicals that carry us gently downward.

A room prepared for sleep is a room prepared for poetry. Keep it cool, for the body surrenders more willingly in a mild chill. Keep it dark, so that even the moon must ask permission to enter. Keep it quiet, or fill the silence with something forgiving—the distant murmur of rain, the low breath of a fan, a melody so soft it dissolves before it becomes thought. Let your bed be a nest of linen and calm, a place where only two things are permitted: dreaming and waking slowly.

But the bed alone cannot save us if the mind arrives bearing suitcases of worry. Before sleep, we must practice the art of letting go. Write the day’s anxieties on a page and leave them there, like letters addressed to tomorrow. Breathe as if each exhale were a small boat drifting out to sea. Forgive the unkind word, the unanswered email, the task half-done. The night does not ask us to be perfect; it asks only that we be present enough to fall.

And do not forget the body, that loyal animal that carries us through daylight. Move it gently during the day so that by evening it is pleasantly tired. Feed it lightly at dusk, avoiding the heavy feast that turns sleep into a battleground. Treat caffeine and alcohol as guests who overstay their welcome—charming at noon, disruptive at night. Let your last cup of tea be herbal, your last hour unhurried.

To improve the quality of sleep is to improve the quality of living. In rest, we are repaired; in dreams, we are made whole. The world will still be there in the morning, urgent and bright. But for now, let the eyelids fall. Let the breath deepen. Trust the darkness. It has never failed to turn, in its own time, into dawn.

---

title: 傲慢与偏见
text:
A Practical Guide to Surviving *Pride and Prejudice*: Or, How to Secure Both Love and £10,000 a Year

*Being a step-by-step manual for readers, romantics, and anyone who has ever misjudged a person at first sight.*

---

 Step 1: Master the Art of the First Impression (Then Distrust It)
Learn to observe, but do not conclude. If a gentleman appears proud, silent, and unwilling to dance, note it—but do not immediately brand him as the worst of men. Conversely, if a charming officer flatters you with stories of woe and injustice, exercise caution. First impressions are data, not verdicts. Mr. Darcy and Mr. Wickham exist to teach us that initial charisma and initial coldness are equally unreliable metrics of character.

 Step 2: Audit the Financials Before the Heart
In the world of *Pride and Prejudice*, romance is a market, and marriage is real estate. Before accepting a proposal, calculate: What is his income? Is the estate entailed away from the female line? Do you possess sufficient fortune to remain independent if you refuse? A practical guide demands practical questions. Remember: love is ideal, but £10,000 a year and a house in Derbyshire are *tangible*.

 Step 3: Identify the Red Flags of Mr. Collinses
Not every suitor who proposes is a prize. Beware the man who:
- Proposes within three days of meeting you.
- Cites the “violence of his affection” while speaking primarily of his patroness’s chimneypiece.
- Frames marriage as a charitable act he is performing upon your family.
Practice the polite but firm refusal. You are not obliged to marry someone merely because they asked first.

 Step 4: Perfect the Lost Art of Letter Writing
When verbal communication fails, write. A well-crafted letter can expose the truth, defend a reputation, and alter the course of an entire novel. Do not dash off emotional texts; instead, compose a measured, honest account of facts and feelings. If you can clear your name and declare your love in the same document, you have achieved epistolary mastery.

 Step 5: Navigate the Assembly Room with Tactical Precision
The ball is the battlefield. Your objectives:
- Secure a dance with the gentleman in question (silence on the dance floor implies silence in the heart).
- Avoid your mother if she is prone to public indiscretion.
- Eavesdrop strategically, but never let your eavesdropping be discovered.
Most importantly: declining a dance says everything. Accepting a dance says more.

 Step 6: Distinguish Between Pride and Prejudice
Conduct a self-audit. Ask yourself honestly:
- Am I acting with prejudice? Am I believing a false narrative because it flatters my ego or confirms my biases?
- Am I acting with pride? Am I refusing to admit I was wrong because my self-regard demands perfection?
You must overcome both to reach your happy ending. Elizabeth must shed her prejudice; Darcy must abandon his pride. You likely need to abandon both.

 Step 7: Survive a Scandal Without Fainting
If a family member elopes with a scoundrel, do not dissolve into hysterics. Action is required. Dispatch the reliable men in your life to London, swallow your pride, and accept help from those you once insulted. A practical guide prioritizes damage control over melodrama. The family name is a currency; protect the exchange rate.

 Step 8: Read the Subtext (Austen Is Never Just Talking About the Weather)
When a character remarks on the fineness of the day, the convenience of the coach, or the beauty of the grounds, they are often making a power move. Listen for irony. If the narrator describes a man as “not a sensible man, and the deficiency of nature had been but little assisted by education or society,” understand that this person is irredeemable. Austen’s narrator is your wisest ally; trust her judgment implicitly.

 Step 9: Walk Three Miles Across Fields to Visit an Ailing Sister
This is both metaphor and instruction. Demonstrate loyalty through action, not just sentiment. Get muddy if necessary. Practical love is inconvenient, unglamorous, and occasionally requires trespassing across gentlemen’s estates. Do it anyway. Character is proven by what you do when no one is watching (or when everyone is watching, and your petticoats are six inches deep in muck).

 Step 10: Accept the Second Proposal
The practical guide acknowledges that timing matters. If you refuse a proposal because you were blinded by error, and the proposer later demonstrates genuine moral growth, reconsider. People can change. Darcy does. Elizabeth does. You do not get extra points for stubborn consistency. The goal is not to be right the first time; the goal is to be right eventually.

 Step 11: Apply These Laws to Modern Life
Translate the Austenian code:
- The assembly room is now the group chat.
- The entail is now student debt or rent in a major city.
- The scandalous elopement is now a regrettable Instagram story.
The principles remain: vet character over charm, communicate with clarity, and never let economic reality override your dignity—or your happiness.

---

Final Note: *Pride and Prejudice* is not ultimately a guide to catching a wealthy husband. It is a guide to becoming a person of independent mind, capable of admitting error and recognizing goodness. Secure your Pemberley if you can, but above all, secure your self-respect.

title: 友谊的价值
text:
The Value of Friendship

Friendship is one of life’s greatest treasures. It is not measured by the number of friends we have, but by the depth of understanding, trust, and care we share with one another. True friendship enriches our lives in ways that money and success cannot.

First, friends provide emotional support. When we face difficulties, a true friend listens without judgment and offers comfort. With friends by our side, problems seem smaller and burdens feel lighter. Knowing that someone genuinely cares gives us the courage to keep going.

Second, friendship helps us grow. Honest friends can point out our weaknesses and encourage us to become better people. They celebrate our successes and remind us of our worth when we doubt ourselves. Through friendship, we learn patience, forgiveness, and the importance of giving as well as receiving.

Finally, friends bring joy to everyday life. Shared laughter, memories, and experiences turn ordinary moments into precious ones. Whether it is a quiet conversation or an exciting adventure, the time spent with friends adds warmth and meaning to our days.

In conclusion, friendship is a priceless gift. It teaches us love, builds our character, and makes life’s journey more beautiful. We should cherish our friends, nurture our relationships, and always be grateful for the valuable role they play in our lives.

title: 培养孩子自主学习习惯
text:
下面是一篇适合睡前朗读的英文童话故事，主题是“培养孩子的自主学习习惯”。

---

 The Little Hedgehog and the Starlight Library

Once upon a time, in a cozy burrow beneath an old oak tree, there lived a little hedgehog named Hazel.

Hazel loved bedtime stories. She loved the ones about brave rabbits, clever foxes, and faraway kingdoms. But when it came time to practice her letters, count acorns, or try puzzles on her own, Hazel would sigh and roll into a prickly ball.

“Mama,” she’d say, “you tell me the answers. Then I’ll know them.”

Mama Hedgehog smiled gently. “If I always tell you, little one, the knowing stays in *my* paws, not yours.”

But Hazel wasn’t sure she believed that.

One soft, moonlit night, after a long day of hiding from her practice book, Hazel wandered outside to look at the stars. She followed a trail of silver light that spilled through the forest and stopped at the old oak tree.

To her surprise, a tiny door glowed in the trunk. Above it, in letters made of stardust, were the words:

“Starlight Library — Open to Those Who Wonder.”

Hazel’s nose twitched. She pushed the door open.

Inside was the most wonderful library she had ever seen. Books floated like fireflies, their pages glowing softly. Spiral staircases wound up into the branches, and everything smelled like cinnamon and old paper.

At the center sat a great gray owl with kind, round eyes.

“Welcome,” said the owl, whose name was Silas. “I am the Keeper of the Starlight Library. What brings you here, little hedgehog?”

Hazel shuffled her paws. “I… I don’t like learning by myself. It’s hard. I want someone else to do the thinking for me.”

Silas nodded slowly. “Then you have come to the right place. Here, books only open when *you* turn the pages. But do not worry — I will sit beside you.”

He led Hazel to a small table and placed a glowing book in front of her.

“The first lesson,” said Silas, “is to begin with a question.”

Hazel looked at the first page. It showed five apples, three baskets, and a sleepy squirrel.

“I don’t know how many apples go in each basket,” Hazel whispered.

“Then ask,” said Silas. “What do you notice? What do you wonder?”

Hazel pointed. “There are five apples. And three baskets. Maybe… I can share them one by one?”

“Try it,” said Silas.

So Hazel drew little apple shapes with her paw on a scrap of paper. One, two, three… then start again. One, two, three.

“Each basket gets one apple,” she said, “and there are two left over!”

The book shimmered, and the words *“Well tried, little learner”* floated off the page like golden dust.

Hazel’s quills stood up with excitement. “I did it — almost by myself!”

“Not almost,” said Silas warmly. “*You* did it. I only helped you start.”

Next, Silas gave her a book of letters. The words were blurry at first, but when Hazel sounded them out slowly — *buh… eh… d* — they became clear.

“Bed,” she said proudly.

The letters twinkled.

Then Silas opened a third book. It was blank.

“This book,” he said, “is for your own ideas. Every night, before sleep, write or draw one thing you learned, or one thing you wonder about. That is how learning grows inside you.”

Hazel took the book in her tiny paws. It felt warm, like a promise.

“But what if I get stuck?” she asked.

“Then you may ask for a hint,” said Silas, “not the answer. And you may rest. A tired brain is like a closed book. Sleep helps the stories sink in.”

Hazel thanked the owl and curled her way back through the glowing door. When she opened her eyes, she was tucked in her own little bed, with moonlight on her quilt.

But on her pillow lay a small, starry notebook.

From that night on, Hazel did her learning a little differently.

When she practiced her letters, she tried first.

When she counted acorns, she worked it out before asking.

When she felt stuck, she asked Mama for *a hint* — not the whole answer.

And every night, before closing her eyes, she wrote or drew one thing in her starry notebook:

*“Today I wondered why the moon changes shape.”*

*“Today I learned that five apples and three baskets leave two apples behind.”*

*“Today I tried, and that was enough.”*

Mama Hedgehog kissed her goodnight. “You are becoming your own teacher, Hazel.”

Hazel yawned, hugging her notebook close.

“Not just my own teacher,” she whispered sleepily. “I’m also my own explorer.”

And with a smile on her face, she drifted into dreams — where books floated like fireflies, and a kind owl waited to help her turn the next page.

The End

---

title: 冬天里的小麻雀
text:
The Little Sparrow in Winter

The first snow had fallen overnight, transforming the village into a silent kingdom of white. Pip, a house sparrow no larger than a child’s clenched fist, huddled on the bare branch of an ancient oak. His feathers, usually puffed with the confident plumpness of autumn, were pressed flat against his quivering body. The north wind cut through the canopy like a knife, and his stomach ached with a hunger that the cold had sharpened into something almost unbearable.

For three days, the frost had tightened its grip. The bakery alley where Pip once found fallen crumbs was now buried beneath a thick, untouched blanket of snow. The community garden, which had offered the last of the wilted sunflower seeds, had become an alien landscape of smooth drifts. Even the hardy berries on the holly bush had been stripped away by flocks of starving starlings the day before. The world had closed its pantry, and winter sat heavy on the land.

Pip chirped once—a thin, trembling note that vanished into the steel-gray sky. He had to move, or the cold would finish what hunger had started. With a desperate flutter, he launched himself into the wind.

Flight had once been a joy. Now it was a battle. The air was dense, pressing against his wings as he crossed the frozen village pond where skaters would soon glide. His vision blurred at the edges, and for a terrifying moment, he felt himself dropping toward the ice. Then, through the swirling snow, he saw it: a square of golden light glowing in the afternoon gloom. A cottage window.

Pip circled above the garden fence, his instincts screaming caution. Winter had taught him that human homes meant danger—cats lurking in doorways, windows that could slam shut, children with quick hands. But then he saw it. On the wooden windowsill, scattered like tiny islands in a white sea, lay bread crumbs. Stale, crusty, impossibly precious bread crumbs.

He landed awkwardly on the sill, his claws scratching for purchase on the frosted wood. The crumbs were stiff with cold but still held the faint memory of yeast and warmth. He pecked ravenously, barely chewing, his entire world narrowing to the miracle of food.

A shadow fell across the glass. Pip froze, crumbs dusting his beak, ready to explode into flight. But it was not a predator. An elderly woman with silver hair stood on the other side of the pane, wrapped in a woolen shawl. She did not bang the glass or call out. She simply smiled—a gentle, crinkled smile of understanding—and tapped her knuckle softly against the window. Then, as if sensing his fear, she stepped back and disappeared into the warm golden room, leaving him to his meal.

Something loosened in Pip’s chest. He was not merely stealing scraps; he was being given a gift. He ate until his belly rounded against his breastbone, then carefully selected one perfect crumb to carry back to the oak tree. With strength returning to his wings like a promise, he flew into the dusk.

That night, as the wind howled through the bare branches and snow piled against the cottage eaves, Pip slept with his head tucked beneath his wing. The crumb lay safe beside him. In the vast, frozen silence of winter, someone had left a light burning and bread upon the sill. And as the sparrow dreamed of budding leaves, he knew he would survive to greet the spring.

title: 活着
text:
以下是《活着》的英文读后感：

---

Living for the Sake of Living: A Reflection on Yu Hua's *To Live*

When I first closed the pages of Yu Hua's *To Live* (活着), I sat in silence for a long time. Few books have left me feeling so heavy-hearted yet strangely at peace. This slim novel, which recounts the life of an ordinary Chinese farmer named Xu Fugui, is one of the most profound meditations on suffering and survival I have ever encountered.

The story begins with Fugui as a spoiled young landlord's son who squanders his family's entire fortune through gambling. This catastrophic loss, however, is only the beginning of his lifelong trial. As China undergoes decades of upheaval—the civil war, land reform, the Great Leap Forward, and the Cultural Revolution—Fugui is forced to endure the deaths of everyone he loves: his parents, his son Youqing, his daughter Fengxia, his devoted wife Jiazhen, his son-in-law Erxi, and finally his little grandson Kugen. By the end of the novel, the old man is left with nothing but an aging ox, with whom he plows the fields and shares his memories.

What struck me most was not the sheer weight of tragedy, but the manner in which Yu Hua tells it. The prose is remarkably plain and restrained. There is no wailing, no dramatic condemnation of fate—only quiet, matter-of-fact narration. This very restraint makes the grief more piercing. When Fugui buries his family members one after another, he weeps, yet he never gives up on living. He simply continues, as the land continues, as the seasons continue.

This leads to the philosophical heart of the novel, which Yu Hua expresses in his preface: "One lives for the sake of living itself, and not for anything outside of living." At first, this statement seemed almost bleak to me. But after finishing the book, I came to understand its depth. Fugui loses wealth, status, and family—everything we normally consider the "meaning" of life—yet he never regards his existence as meaningless. His capacity to keep going, to find small comforts in his ox and his old songs, is itself a form of quiet heroism. The novel suggests that life does not need to be justified by external achievements or happiness; the act of living, with all its pain and impermanence, carries its own dignity.

The final scene lingers in my mind: an old man and an old ox walking slowly into the dusk, the man's rough singing echoing across the empty fields. There is sorrow in this image, but also an unexpected serenity. Fugui has made peace with his fate—not through indifference, but through acceptance. He remembers his loved ones with tenderness rather than bitterness.

Reading *To Live* changed the way I think about hardship. In modern life, we often measure existence by success, comfort, and recognition, and we despair when these are threatened. Fugui's story reminds me that the meaning of life may be far simpler and more fundamental: to cherish those around us while we can, to endure what cannot be changed, and to greet each new day—however ordinary—as something worth living for. As Yu Hua writes, life belongs to each person's own feelings, not to anyone else's judgment.

This is a book that breaks your heart and then, gently, teaches you how to live with the pieces.

---

title: 健康饮食
text:
The Alchemy of Nourishment

To eat well is to conduct a quiet conversation with one's own body—a dialogue spoken not in words, but in colors, textures, and the subtle alchemy of nutrients dancing through the bloodstream. In a world that often confuses nourishment with mere fuel, the art of healthy eating remains a forgotten poetry, waiting to be recited at the dinner table.

Consider the marketplace at dawn, where nature displays its edible palette. The deep violet of eggplant, the sunburst orange of persimmons, the emerald arrogance of spinach—these are not merely ingredients, but the earth's love letters, pressed in chlorophyll and sweetness. To choose them is to accept an invitation to vitality, to align oneself with the ancient rhythm of seasons rather than the industrial hum of convenience.

There is a peculiar intimacy in preparing food with one's own hands. The crisp surrender of a knife through bell pepper, the fragrant exhale of herbs beneath a rolling pin, the slow transformation of raw elements into sustenance—these acts compose a meditation more restorative than any pill. The body, that faithful vessel which carries us through decades of sunrises, deserves more than the gray anonymity of processed packages. It remembers the kindness of olive oil, the loyalty of whole grains, the exuberance of berries still warm from the vine.

And yet, healthy eating is not a monastery of deprivation. It is not about shrinking oneself into arbitrary numbers or banishing joy from the plate. Rather, it is an expansion—a broadening of awareness to recognize that every bite is either a step toward bloom or a slide toward wither. When we eat mindfully, we discover that a perfectly ripe peach contains more drama than any confectionery, that the earthy complexity of quinoa satisfies deeper than the hollow thrill of empty calories.

To nourish oneself properly is, ultimately, an act of reverence. It is the acknowledgment that we are composed of what we consume, quite literally—that our thoughts, our stamina, the very luminosity of our skin, are sculpted by the choices we make three times a day. In the quiet ceremony of a wholesome meal, we practice a radical form of self-respect. We say to ourselves: *you are worth the good oil, the fresh leaf, the unhurried preparation.*

So let us eat not merely to silence hunger, but to celebrate the astonishing privilege of being alive. Let our plates be canvases of intention, our meals pauses of gratitude in the rushing narrative of our days. For in the end, the body does not ask for perfection—it asks for presence, for color, for care. And when we answer with whole foods and whole hearts, we do not just feed ourselves. We flourish.

title: 家庭理财
text:
A Practical Guide to Family Financial Management

Managing household finances doesn't have to be overwhelming. Follow these steps to build a solid financial foundation for your family.

 Step 1: Assess Your Current Financial Situation

- Calculate your total income: Include salaries, bonuses, side hustles, and any passive income.
- Track your spending: Review bank statements and receipts from the past 2–3 months to see where your money goes.
- Determine your net worth: List all assets (savings, property, investments) and subtract all liabilities (loans, credit card debt, mortgages).

 Step 2: Set Clear Financial Goals

- Short-term goals (within 1 year): e.g., build a small emergency cushion, pay off a credit card.
- Mid-term goals (1–5 years): e.g., save for a down payment, buy a car, fund a family vacation.
- Long-term goals (5+ years): e.g., retirement savings, children's education fund, paying off the mortgage.
- Make goals SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

 Step 3: Create a Realistic Budget

- Try the 50/30/20 rule:
  - 50% for needs (housing, food, utilities, transportation)
  - 30% for wants (dining out, entertainment, hobbies)
  - 20% for savings and debt repayment
- Use budgeting apps or a simple spreadsheet to monitor categories.
- Hold a monthly family meeting to review spending together.

 Step 4: Build an Emergency Fund

- Aim for 3–6 months of essential living expenses.
- Start small—even $500–$1,000 can cover minor emergencies.
- Keep it in a separate, easily accessible high-yield savings account.

 Step 5: Tackle Debt Strategically

- List all debts with balances, interest rates, and minimum payments.
- Choose a payoff method:
  - Avalanche method: Pay off the highest-interest debt first (saves the most money).
  - Snowball method: Pay off the smallest balance first (builds momentum and motivation).
- Avoid taking on new high-interest debt while paying off existing balances.

 Step 6: Save and Invest for the Future

- Pay yourself first: Automate transfers to savings and investment accounts on payday.
- Take advantage of retirement accounts: Contribute enough to get any employer match—it's free money.
- Invest for growth: Low-cost index funds are a simple, diversified option for beginners.
- Start an education fund: If you have children, consider a dedicated college savings plan.

 Step 7: Protect Your Family with Insurance

- Health insurance: Essential to avoid catastrophic medical bills.
- Life insurance: Especially important if others depend on your income (a common guideline is 10× your annual income).
- Disability insurance: Protects your income if you can't work.
- Home/renters and auto insurance: Review coverage annually for adequacy and better rates.

 Step 8: Plan for Major Expenses

- Anticipate big costs—weddings, home repairs, car replacement, holidays—and save for them in sinking funds.
- This prevents surprise expenses from derailing your budget or forcing you into debt.

 Step 9: Get Your Estate in Order

- Write a will and update it after major life events (marriage, birth, divorce).
- Name beneficiaries on all financial accounts and insurance policies.
- Consider setting up powers of attorney and a healthcare directive.

 Step 10: Review and Adjust Regularly

- Monthly: Check your budget and spending.
- Quarterly: Review savings progress and investment performance.
- Annually: Reassess goals, insurance coverage, and your overall financial plan.
- Life changes—your plan should too.

---

Key principle to remember: Consistency beats perfection. Small, regular steps—saving a little each month, spending mindfully, reviewing often—compound into lasting financial security for your family.

title: 会说话的大树
text:
The Oak Who Spoke

When Maya moved to her grandmother's old farmhouse, she was certain she would hate everything about it. No friends, no Wi-Fi in the backyard, nothing but fields and one enormous oak tree that leaned over the garden like a tired giant.

She was sitting beneath it one July afternoon, picking at the grass, when a voice rumbled above her head.

"You're pulling up my toes."

Maya froze. The voice was deep and slow, like stones grinding together at the bottom of a river.

"Who said that?"

"I did," said the oak. "Down here. Well—up here. All of me, really."

Most children would have run screaming. Maya, who had read too many books about magic to be properly surprised, simply looked up into the rustling leaves and said, "Trees can't talk."

"And girls can't hear them," the oak replied. "Yet here we are."

His name, he told her, was Alder—which was confusing, since he was an oak, but he explained that names chosen at four hundred years old tend to stick. He had grown from an acorn planted by her great-great-great-grandmother, and he had watched the farm change hands, watched storms come and go, watched children grow into old people who no longer climbed his branches.

Maya visited him every day. Alder told her about the winter the creek froze solid and deer walked across it like ballerinas. He told her about the boy who carved his initials into Alder's bark in 1932 and returned sixty years later, grey-haired, with a granddaughter who became Maya's grandmother.

"Trees remember everything," Alder said. "We just remember it slowly."

In September, men in yellow vests came with clipboards. Maya's grandmother explained gently that the oak was hollow at the heart and might fall on the house in a storm. It had to come down.

Maya cried beneath his branches that evening.

"Don't," Alder rumbled. "Four hundred years is a good long life. I've been lucky."

"But I'll lose you!"

"Silly girl." His leaves shivered, though there was no wind. "Look beneath the third root on the east side."

There, nestled in the soil, Maya found a small green sapling, no taller than her hand.

"My last gift," Alder said. "Plant it somewhere with good light. It won't speak for a long, long time—trees learn their words slowly, the way you learned yours. But one day—" his voice grew softer, like leaves settling, "—one day, a child will sit beneath it, feeling alone in a new place. And it will know exactly what to say."

They took the old oak down in October. Maya planted the sapling on the hill where the morning sun touched first.

It hasn't spoken yet. But Maya is patient. She waters it, reads to it, and waits.

After all, some things are worth waiting four hundred years for.

title: 海底两万里
text:
Book Review: *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea*  

Reading Jules Verne’s *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea* felt like being invited on a voyage to a world I had never truly imagined. Published in 1870, the novel follows Professor Pierre Aronnax, his loyal servant Conseil, and the Canadian harpooner Ned Land as they are taken aboard the *Nautilus*, a futuristic submarine commanded by the mysterious Captain Nemo. What follows is not merely a journey across the oceans, but a deep dive into the wonders, dangers, and mysteries of the underwater world.

What struck me most was Verne’s incredible imagination. Long before submarines became common, he described a vessel capable of traveling beneath the waves, powered by electricity and filled with scientific wonders. Reading about the *Nautilus* gliding through coral gardens, past shipwrecks, and under the ice of Antarctica made me feel as if I were looking through a glass window into the ocean myself. Verne’s detailed descriptions of sea creatures and underwater landscapes show both his scientific knowledge and his love for nature.

Captain Nemo is another fascinating part of the novel. He is brilliant, rich, and free, yet he is also lonely and filled with anger toward the world above the sea. His character made me think about the price of freedom and the danger of isolation. Nemo escapes society, but he cannot escape his own pain. Through him, Verne asks an important question: Can a person truly live apart from the rest of humanity?

The relationship among the characters also added depth to the story. Aronnax is curious and eager to learn, Conseil is calm and devoted, and Ned Land longs for freedom and home. Their different reactions to life on the *Nautilus* made me reflect on how people respond differently to the same situation.

Overall, *Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea* is more than an adventure story. It is a celebration of human curiosity, a warning about the destructive power of hatred, and a reminder of the beauty hidden beneath the surface of our world. After reading it, I found myself looking at the ocean with new eyes, wondering what secrets still remain in its depths. Verne’s novel proves that exploration—whether of the sea or of the human heart—is a journey worth taking.
